title: Derived-functor criterion and comparison maps in finitely many variables
statement:
Fix $1\le n\le4$. For $1\le i\le n$ let $A_i$ be a category [def-nagata-category], $W_i$ a class of arrows containing identities, $L_i:A_i\to D_i$ a localization, and $P_i\subseteq A_i$ a full subcategory whose inclusion is a left derivability structure [def-sfb-left-derivability-structure]. The product inclusion $\prod_iP_i\to\prod_iA_i$ is a left derivability structure for the product arrow class consisting of tuples $(w_i)_i$ with $w_i\in W_i$ for every $i$, and $L=\prod_iL_i$ is a localization of that class. The full subcategory $P_i=A_i$ with identity inclusion is permitted and is a left derivability structure. Let $H$ be any category and $F:\prod_iA_i\to H$ a functor whose restriction to $\prod_iP_i$ sends each coordinate $W_i$-arrow to an isomorphism when the other coordinates lie in their $P_j$. Then there exist $LF:\prod_iD_i\to H$ and $\varepsilon:LF\circ L\Rightarrow F$ that are a total left derived functor in all $n$ variables: for every $V:\prod_iD_i\to H$, composition with $\varepsilon$ gives a bijection
$$ \operatorname{Nat}(V,LF)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Nat}(V\circ L,F). $$
For a candidate $(T,\eta:T\circ L\Rightarrow F)$, this universal property holds if and only if every $\eta_{(P_1,\ldots,P_n)}$ is an isomorphism. In particular the counit of $LF$ is invertible there. If $G$ satisfies the same hypotheses with chosen $(LG,\varepsilon_G)$ and $\tau:F\Rightarrow G$, there is a unique $L\tau:LF\Rightarrow LG$ with
$$ (\varepsilon_G)_x\circ(L\tau)_{Lx}=\tau_x\circ\varepsilon_x $$
for every tuple $x$ of objects of the $A_i$. This operation preserves identities and composition and sends natural isomorphisms to natural isomorphisms. For arbitrary $V$, maps $\gamma_1,\gamma_2:V\Rightarrow LF$ are equal if $\varepsilon\circ(\gamma_1 L)=\varepsilon\circ(\gamma_2 L)$. More generally, natural transformations between any two functors on $\prod_iD_i$ are determined by their components at tuples $(L_1P_1,\ldots,L_nP_n)$.

source.place: Proof, sentences on the two-variable derived functor, iterated tensor products in three and four variables, and descending constraints

proof.text: Write $W_i^P=i_i^{-1}W_i$ and choose the localizations $L_i^P:P_i\to D_i^P$ appearing in the derivability structures. The inverse-image classes contain identities because the $W_i$ do. Apply [lem-sfb-product-localization] twice: $L=\prod_i L_i$ localizes $A=\prod_i A_i$ at $W=\prod_iW_i$, and $L_P=\prod_iL_i^P$ localizes $P=\prod_iP_i$ at $W_P=\prod_iW_i^P$. Thus the localization data for the product inclusion can be taken to be these products, with $E=\prod_iE_i$ and the product of the coordinate comparison isomorphisms.

source.place: Proof, finite-variable localization underlying descent of tensor products

proof.text: Check the two conditions of [def-sfb-left-derivability-structure] for $i=\prod_i i_i$. Given $X=(X_i)_i$, choose $r_i:i_iP_i\to X_i$ in $W_i$; their tuple is in $W$. For finality, fix an object $(Y,b)$ of $(E\downarrow LX)$. It is a tuple $(Y_i,b_i)$, and its category of triples $(P,a,c)$ in the cited definition is exactly the product of the coordinate triple categories: the two equations defining arrows are coordinatewise. Each factor is nonempty and connected by coordinate finality. Choose an object in each factor to obtain a product object. Given two product objects, join their first coordinates by a finite zigzag, using identities in all other coordinates; then do this for the second coordinate and so on. There are only $n$ coordinates, so concatenation is a finite zigzag connecting the two product objects. This proves nonemptiness and connectedness, hence the required finality.

source.place: Proof, the derivability structure used for tensor descent, expanded coordinatewise

proof.text: For the identity inclusion $P_i=A_i$, choose $L_i^P=L_i$ and $E_i=\operatorname{id}_{D_i}$. The resolution of $X$ is $\operatorname{id}_X$, which belongs to $W_i$. For an object $(Y,b:Y\to L_iX)$, its triple category has terminal object $(X,\operatorname{id}_X,b)$: the unique arrow from $(P,a,c)$ to it is $a$, and its second required equation is precisely $L_i(a)c=b$. A category with a terminal object is nonempty and connected, since each object maps to that object. This proves the identity-inclusion assertion directly from [def-sfb-left-derivability-structure].

source.place: Proof, inclusion of unchanged arguments when deriving iterated tensor products

proof.text: The restriction of $F$ to $P=\prod_iP_i$ inverts $W_P$. Indeed any tuple $(w_i)_i$ factors into the $n$ arrows changing one coordinate at a time. Every intermediate object remains in $P$, all identity coordinates belong to their $W_j$, and $F$ sends each factor to an isomorphism by the stated coordinate hypothesis. Its image of the tuple is their composite, hence invertible. Apply [lem-sfb-unary-left-derived-calculus] with $A,P,W,D,L$ the product data established above. Its existence assertion gives $LF$ and $\varepsilon$ with the displayed bijection. Its candidate criterion gives precisely invertibility of $\eta$ on tuples of resolving objects, and gives this invertibility for $\varepsilon$ itself.

source.place: Proof, two-variable derived functor and its extension to three and four variables

proof.text: Apply the universal bijection for $(LG,\varepsilon_G)$, supplied by [lem-sfb-unary-left-derived-calculus] with $G$ in place of $F$, to the test functor $V=LF$ and the transformation $\tau\circ\varepsilon:LF\circ L\Rightarrow G$. It gives the unique $L\tau:LF\Rightarrow LG$ with $\varepsilon_G\circ((L\tau)L)=\tau\circ\varepsilon$. For an identity $\tau$, the identity on $LF$ satisfies this equation, so uniqueness gives $L(\operatorname{id})=\operatorname{id}$. For $\sigma:G\Rightarrow K$, composing the defining equations yields $\varepsilon_K\circ(((L\sigma)\circ(L\tau))L)=(\sigma\circ\tau)\circ\varepsilon$, so uniqueness for $LK$ gives $L(\sigma\circ\tau)=(L\sigma)\circ(L\tau)$. If $\tau$ is invertible, apply this result to $\tau^{-1}\tau$ and $\tau\tau^{-1}$ to obtain inverse transformations $L\tau$ and $L(\tau^{-1})$.

source.place: Proof, descending constraints and their comparison maps via universal properties

proof.text: For arbitrary $V$, the universal bijection of [lem-sfb-unary-left-derived-calculus] sends $\gamma:V\Rightarrow LF$ to $\varepsilon\circ(\gamma L)$. If two such composites agree, injectivity of this bijection gives $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$.

Let $\gamma,\delta:V\Rightarrow V'$ agree at every tuple $(L_iP_i)_i$. Given $y=(y_i)_i$, [lem-trf-localization-essentially-surjective] supplies $a_i\in A_i$ and isomorphisms $L_i a_i\cong y_i$. The resolution clause of [def-sfb-left-derivability-structure] supplies $r_i:i_iP_i\to a_i$ in $W_i$. Since $L_i$ inverts $W_i$, composing these isomorphisms gives $u:(L_iP_i)_i\xrightarrow{\sim}y$. Write $z=(L_iP_i)_i$. Naturality gives $\gamma_y V(u)=V'(u)\gamma_z=V'(u)\delta_z=\delta_y V(u)$. Cancel the isomorphism $V(u)$ to get $\gamma_y=\delta_y$ for every $y$, and hence equality of transformations. All uses of resolutions are valid also for $n=1$ or identity inclusions.
